name: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease, UMOD-related

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by variants in UMOD, which encodes uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), the predominant protein of normal urine, synthesised only in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
Early hyperuricaemia and gout, often appearing in adolescence or young adulthood and disproportionate to the degree of renal impairment, are the most characteristic clues.
Urinalysis is typically bland with minimal proteinuria and little or no haematuria, which can falsely reassure the clinician.
The fractional excretion of urate is inappropriately low for the level of serum urate, reflecting avid tubular urate reabsorption.
Kidneys are normal-sized or small; medullary or corticomedullary cysts may be present but are not required for the diagnosis.
Most pathogenic variants are missense changes affecting conserved cysteine residues, causing uromodulin misfolding and endoplasmic reticulum retention within tubular cells.
Diagnosis rests on targeted genetic testing supported by a family history of dominantly inherited chronic kidney disease and premature gout.
The disease does not recur after kidney transplantation, so grafting is an effective long-term option.
reference.pathophysiology: UMOD encodes uromodulin, a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored glycoprotein produced exclusively by epithelial cells of the thick ascending limb and early distal convoluted tubule. Most disease-causing variants are missense changes that alter conserved cysteine residues within the calcium-binding domains, disrupting disulphide bonding and causing the protein to misfold. Rather than trafficking to the apical membrane, misfolded uromodulin is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering the unfolded protein response, chronic endoplasmic reticulum stress and progressive tubular injury, with reduced urinary uromodulin excretion. Impaired uromodulin handling disturbs thick ascending limb transport (including the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransport apparatus), promoting subtle salt wasting and volume contraction that secondarily enhance proximal urate reabsorption; this manifests as a low fractional excretion of urate with early hyperuricaemia and gout. Over years the accumulated tubular stress drives interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, producing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other ADTKD subtypes (MUC1, REN, HNF1B, SEC61A1)
Primary gout with chronic urate nephropathy
Alport syndrome and other hereditary nephropathies (usually with haematuria)
additionalInvestigations: Serum urate together with fractional excretion of urate
Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and medullary or corticomedullary cysts
Targeted UMOD sequencing or a dedicated ADTKD gene panel
Renal biopsy with uromodulin immunostaining showing tubular endoplasmic reticulum retention, when biopsy is performed
redFlags: Gout in adolescence or early adulthood, especially with a family history of kidney failure
Progressive chronic kidney disease with a persistently bland urinary sediment
Family history of dominantly inherited end-stage kidney disease of unexplained cause
Rapidly worsening renal function suggesting a superimposed insult
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive chronic kidney disease reaching the end stage in adulthood, with wide variation in the age of onset within and between affected families. Kidney transplantation is effective because the disease does not recur in the allograft.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as primary gout and missing the underlying hereditary kidney disease
Being falsely reassured by bland urine and normal-sized kidneys
Expecting cysts to be present, when their absence does not exclude the diagnosis
Assuming urate-lowering therapy will halt renal progression, for which evidence is lacking
references: Consensus guidance on autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
management: Initiate urate-lowering therapy with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor such as allopurinol or febuxostat early to control hyperuricaemia and prevent recurrent gout, even before significant renal impairment
Treat acute gout flares with colchicine or corticosteroids, using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cautiously given the renal impairment
Provide general chronic kidney disease care with blood pressure control, avoidance of nephrotoxins and management of cardiovascular risk
Encourage adequate salt and fluid intake and avoid volume depletion, since impaired thick ascending limb transport predisposes to salt wasting
Monitor renal function, serum urate and blood pressure at regular intervals to track progression
Plan renal replacement therapy as disease advances, with kidney transplantation preferred because the disorder does not recur in the allograft
Offer genetic counselling and cascade UMOD testing to at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
Refer to nephrology with clinical genetics input for confirmatory testing and family assessment
